Notes: Year Established -860 (c.): Encyclopaedia Judaica says the city 'was rebuilt by Hiel, the Bethelite, in the days of Ahab' (I Kings 16:34; Ahab's reign c. 871-852 BCE, midpoint used), the earliest documented Israelite settlement at Jericho; it also states the city 'expanded considerably at the end of the Israelite period (seventh, sixth centuries)' but 'remained unfortified and unimportant up to its destruction by the Babylonians in 587 B.C.E.' Event row: Babylonian destruction of Judahite Jericho, 587/586 BCE. Population blank: the source does not say no Jews remained.

Ancient figure accepted by the source: Encyclopaedia Judaica states 'The city was resettled by 345 Babylonian exiles (Neh. 7:36)' (= Ezra 2:34, 'the sons of Jericho - 345'). Year c. 538 BCE (return under Cyrus; the date of the list of returnees is debated - Finkelstein, PEQ 140 (2008), argues it reflects the Hasmonean period). Treated as resident returnees settled at Jericho.

Nehemiah 3:2: 'Next to him, a [work] party from Jericho built' (Hebrew 'anshei Yereho') - men of Jericho rebuilt a section of the Jerusalem wall under Nehemiah, c. 445 BCE. Attests an organized Judean community at Jericho in the Persian period; no count.

Persian period (539-332 BCE, midpoint -435). Encyclopaedia Judaica: 'A small settlement existed there in the post-Exilic period'; jar handles inscribed 'Yehud' (Aramaic name of the Persian province of Judea), one also naming 'Urio', indicate Jericho belonged to the Judean province. Presence of a small Judean settlement; no count.

Event (c.): Livius chronology: '347 BCE: Achaemenid campaign against Nectanebo II; Jericho destroyed and Jews were deported to Hyrcania' (echoed in the book of Judith per the source). Population blank: the source does not state that no Jews remained; scale of the deportation unknown.

Event (c. 160 BCE): 1 Maccabees 9:50 - the Seleucid general Bacchides 'built strong cities in Judea: the fortress in Jericho'. Seleucid fortification of Jericho during the Maccabean wars; Jericho counted among the cities of Judea. No count.

Event, 134 BCE: 1 Maccabees 16:11-16 - Ptolemy son of Abubus, son-in-law of the high priest Simon, 'had been appointed governor over the plain of Jericho'; he murdered Simon and two of his sons at a banquet in the stronghold of Dok near Jericho. Attests Hasmonean (Jewish) administration of the Jericho district; no count.

Hasmonean palace at Tulul Abu el-Alayiq 'built by John Hyrcanus I (134-104 BCE)' (midpoint -119, c.), fortified under Alexander Jannaeus; 'Many ritual baths were found around the palace', linked to priestly owners eating terumah in purity, plus a ritual bath for vessels with remains of 800 bowls. Jewish (Hasmonean royal/priestly) presence with miqvaot; no count. Wikipedia used as last resort; underlying source Netzer's final reports.

Hasmonean period (140-37 BCE, midpoint -90). Joshua Schwartz (quoted by Aish): 'the fertility of the Jericho area as well as its administrative importance apparently attracted a priestly population' early in the Second Temple period, and 'the priestly population of Jericho grew when the area was developed by the Hasmoneans who built royal estates there'; funerary caves indicate a priestly community. Presence of a sizeable priestly community; no count.

c. 75 BCE: D. Stacey (Bible and Interpretation, 2001): next to the hall Netzer called a synagogue lay 'a row of perhaps ten houses' which 'probably housed the chief officials of the estate'; 'The mikveh, or ritual bath, built on the south side of the hall, was a common feature of Hasmonean Jericho'; 'we do not know where the estate workers and the general population of Jericho lived.' Stacey disputes the synagogue identification. About ten houses of estate officials - not a count of the town's Jews, so Population blank.

Synagogue (identification debated): NEAEHL (Netzer) - administrators' buildings dated to the end of Alexander Jannaeus' reign; 'In the second phase, probably during the reign of Queen Salome Alexandra (76-67 BCE), this building was turned into a synagogue', with a mikveh of two pools; the workshop area 'also included several mikvehs'. Year = midpoint of 76-67 BCE (c.). Suggests an organized Jewish community serving the royal estate; no count.

Event, c. 57 BCE: Josephus, War 1.170 - Gabinius divided the Jewish nation into five districts (conventions/synedria), 'a fourth to Jericho'. Jericho was the seat of one of the five Jewish councils of Judea; no count.

Event, 39/38 BCE: Josephus, War 1.299-302 - Herod reached Jericho and 'found the city deserted, but that there were five hundred men, with their wives and children' (who had fled to the heights and were captured); the Romans plundered the city, finding 'the houses full of all sorts of good things', and Herod left a garrison. The 500 men are captives/refugees, not a resident count, so Population blank; the full houses imply a substantial (Jewish) town.

Event, 31 BCE: Netzer et al. 2001 (quoted): 'The synagogue complex at Jericho was apparently built in order to serve the residents in the nearby buildings (Area AH)'; 'The Synagogue Complex was probably destroyed during the earthquake of 31 B.C.E., or slightly later, as a deliberate act'; Herod's Second Palace was then built over it. Residents present but no count.

Jewish necropolis of Jericho (Hachlili's excavation): a cemetery spanning seven hills with 'approximately 120 excavated and surveyed tomb-caves'; 'The tombs encompass a 150-year period that ended when the Romans destroyed Jericho in 68 A.D.' (c. 82 BCE-68 CE; midpoint used). Includes the Goliath family tomb, the largest; a study of its skeletons (Smith and Arensburg) found 23% of adults over 50. Indicates a large, long-lived Jewish community; no count given.
Event, 4 BCE: Josephus, War 2.57 - after Herod's death, the rebel Simon of Peraea 'burnt down the royal palace that was at Jericho, and many other costly edifices besides'. No count.

Early Roman period (63 BCE-70 CE, midpoint 4; pre-70 conditions). Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), Jericho: Jericho furnished a priestly group for each of the 24 courses, 'but half as numerous' as Jerusalem's (Yer. Ta'an. 4:2; cf. Ta'an. 27a, where half of each watch went up from Jericho), and Jericho had 'a large priestly population'. Rabbinic tradition of a large resident priestly community; no number of persons.

c. 30 CE: Luke 19:1-9 - at Jericho 'A man was there named Zacchaeus; he was a chief tax collector and was rich', called 'a son of Abraham' (a Jewish resident with a house in Jericho). Named Jewish individual; no count.

Ossuary inscription IIP JERI0001 (Hebrew/Aramaic): 'Yehosef, son of Yitro(?)'; soft limestone Jewish ossuary from Jericho dated 5-70 CE (midpoint 38, c.). Named Jewish individual; part of the Jericho Jewish cemetery.

Ossuary burials at Jericho: Encyclopaedia Judaica (Avi-Yonah and Gibson): 'Ossuaries found by Hachlili at Jericho are dated to a more restricted time period: 10-68 c.e.' (midpoint 39). Jewish secondary burial in ossuaries; community-scale cemetery; no count.

1st c. CE (midpoint 50; Mishnah on pre-70 conditions). Mishnah Pesachim 4:8: 'Six actions were performed by the Jewish residents of Jericho, contrary to common practice' (grafting palms on 14 Nisan, etc.), some reprimanded by the Sages. Attests an established Jewish community at Jericho with its own customs; no count.

c. 60 CE (after Agrippina married Claudius, 49 CE): ossuary in the Goliath family tomb inscribed 'Theodotus, freedman of Queen Agrippina'; BAS: Theodotus = Nathanel, father of 'Mariah daughter of Nathanel'; 'Sometime after his return to Jericho, he died and was buried with his family.' Named Jewish individual (a returned freedman) and his family.

c. 66 CE: Josephus, War 3.55 - Jericho is listed among the cities presiding over the toparchies of Judea ('and Herodium, and Jericho'). Jericho a Jewish district capital at the outbreak of the revolt; no count.

Event, 68 CE: Josephus, War 4.450-452 - as Vespasian approached, 'a great multitude ... came out of Jericho, and fled to those mountainous parts' over against Jerusalem, 'while that part which was left behind was in a great measure destroyed'; the Romans 'found the city desolate'. Population 0 = Josephus' statement that the city was deserted (residents fled or were killed); the BAS/Hachlili cemetery dating also ends with the Roman destruction of Jericho in 68 CE.

Event, 68/69 CE: Josephus, War 4.486 - Vespasian 'erected citadels at Jericho and Adida, and placed garrisons in them both'. Roman garrison (not Jewish residents) at the deserted site; Population blank.
